abstract: Belonogaster is an African genus of primitively eusocial wasps. They are widespread and conspicuous across sub-Saharan Africa and yet are among the least studied groups of social wasps. Here, we present the first high-quality, chromosome-level genome assembly for a representative of this genus, Belonogaster juncea, complemented by an RNA-seq analysis of brain transcription among individuals representing reproductive and non-reproductive castes. The assembled genome spans 315.8 Mb with a scaffold N50 of 7.91 Mb. The annotation contained 15,159 protein-coding genes and 20,046 isoforms, with Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) completeness of 98.0% for the genome and 97.8% for the annotation. Using this new assembly, we show that the B. juncea genome differs notably from other social wasp genomes: a single satellite repeat makes up a fifth of its chromosome-scale sequence, it has the highest putative chromosome number in a sequenced wasp genome to date, and it shows high levels of syntenic breaks. We find caste neuro-transcription differences between queens and workers, revealing 573 differentially expressed genes (341 worker biased, 232 queen biased), with significant overlap in caste-specific genes when compared to Polistes dominula and Liostenogaster flavolineata. This genomic resource provides a foundation for understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying primitive eusociality and social evolution in wasps, and opens up new research opportunities for a genus of little-studied insects from the Global South.
